entry.content:

A robot vacuum leaves its dock, cleans every room and drives back to the dock. A warehouse robot carries a shelf across a building full of people. A delivery robot crosses a campus. None of them follows a painted line. Each one keeps answering the same few questions, many times a second: where am I, what is around me, where should I go, and how do I get there?

This series builds the answers from the ground up. We start with a wheel and a motor, and finish with a robot that maps a room it has never seen and plans its way through it. Along the way come the parts people actually buy: encoders, IMUs, an ESP32 microcontroller, a Raspberry Pi or NVIDIA Jetson computer, lidar, depth cameras, and the software that ties them together, ROS 2.

Every figure runs a simulated robot in a simulated room, in your browser. The robot has the same wheels, the same encoders and the same sensor noise from part to part, so the drift you see in part 4 is the drift the Kalman filter fixes in part 12. Every number quoted in the text is computed by the same code.

This first part sets up the vocabulary: what a mobile robot is made of, how we write down where it is, and how it relates what its sensors see to the room around it.

The robot we’ll build

The robot in this series is the kind people build at home or in a university lab:

  • a round body with two driven wheels, one on each side, and a free-turning caster wheel to keep it level;
  • two small DC gear motors with encoders, which count how far each wheel has turned;
  • an IMU (gyroscope and accelerometer), a 360° lidar, and later a depth camera;
  • an ESP32 microcontroller that drives the motors and reads the encoders in real time;
  • a Raspberry Pi or Jetson that runs ROS 2, builds the map and plans the route.

Its wheels are 70 mm across and 220 mm apart, and each encoder gives 1,320 counts per turn of the wheel. We’ll see where those numbers come from in parts 2 and 4.

Where the robot is, step by step

Every robot runs one loop. It senses: reads its encoders, its IMU, its lidar. It thinks: updates what it believes about itself and the room, and decides what to do. It acts: sends speeds to its motors.

Then the world answers. The wheels slip a little, a person walks past, the floor turns to carpet. The next turn of the loop has to deal with whatever happened.

The loop runs at different speeds for different jobs. Motor control runs hundreds or thousands of times a second, on the microcontroller. Building a map runs a few times a second, on the bigger computer. This series climbs the loop from the bottom: motors and encoders first, maps and plans last.

This is the room the robot lives in, seen from above: 10 m by 6 m, with a box, a table, a short wall, a pillar and a cabinet. The origin is the bottom-left corner. \(x\) points right, \(y\) points up.

A robot on a flat floor can be anywhere in the room and face any way. Three numbers say which: its position \(x\) and \(y\) in metres, and its heading \(\theta\), the angle from the \(x\) axis, counted anticlockwise. Together they are its pose:

\[\text{pose} = (x, y, \theta) = (1.20\ \text{m},\ 0.90\ \text{m},\ 20^\circ)\]

Drag the slider to turn the robot. Its position stays put; only \(\theta\) changes. Most robotics code stores \(\theta\) in radians, from \(-\pi\) to \(\pi\).

Sensors don’t know where the robot is. A lidar on the robot reports what it sees relative to itself: “something 1.57 m away, a little to my left”. It describes the world in the robot’s frame: \(x'\) points straight ahead, \(y'\) points to the robot’s left.

The corner of the box, P, is at (2.60, 1.60) in the room. In the robot’s frame it is at (1.55, 0.18): 1.55 m ahead and 18 cm to the left.

To go from the room to the robot’s frame, subtract the robot’s position, then rotate by \(-\theta\):

\[\begin{aligned} x' &= \cos\theta\,\Delta x + \sin\theta\,\Delta y \\ y' &= -\sin\theta\,\Delta x + \cos\theta\,\Delta y \end{aligned}\]

Here \(\Delta x = 1.40\), \(\Delta y = 0.70\), \(\cos 20^\circ = 0.940\) and \(\sin 20^\circ = 0.342\), which gives \(x' = 1.55\) and \(y' = 0.18\). Turn the robot with the slider: P’s room coordinates never change, but its coordinates in the robot’s frame do.

Now let it drive. The robot rolls forward at 0.3 m/s while turning left, for 6 seconds. Scroll to move it along.

P never moves in the room. In the robot’s frame it slides past: from 1.55 m ahead at the start, to (−0.76, −0.44) at the end, behind the robot and to its right.

This is the whole problem of a mobile robot in miniature. Its sensors measure the world in its own moving frame. To build a map, or to follow one, it has to know its own pose, so it can carry every measurement over into the room’s frame.

A real robot has more than two frames. The lidar isn’t at the robot’s centre. On our robot it sits 8 cm ahead of it, so it has a frame of its own, laser. The robot’s frame is called base_link.

ROS, the software we’ll use from part 10, names the frames of a wheeled robot by a shared convention, REP 105:

  • map: fixed to the room;
  • odom: where the robot’s wheel odometry started counting;
  • base_link: fixed to the robot;
  • one frame per sensor, here laser.

Each link in the chain is one pose. To put a lidar point on the map, apply the links one by one: P is at (1.47, 0.18) from the lidar, (1.55, 0.18) from the robot’s centre, and (2.60, 1.60) on the map.

Why are there both map and odom? The robot works out its pose by counting wheel turns, called odometry (part 4). Odometry is smooth and fast, but every small error adds up.

Here the robot drives a 2.5 m square, and its right wheel is just 0.4% bigger than the software thinks. Its track is 1% wider. After 40 seconds, odometry says the robot is back where it started, at (1.00, 0.80). It is really at (1.17, 0.65), turned 7.5°: 23 cm away.

So the robot keeps two estimates. odom → base_link is the smooth one from the wheels, which drifts. map → odom is the correction that something smarter, a localiser or SLAM, keeps adjusting so that the chain ends at the true pose. Here that correction is (0.28, −0.27, 7.5°). Parts 12 to 14 are about computing it.

Frames in one line

A pose \(a = (x, y, \theta)\) is also a transform: it takes a point \(p\) given in the robot’s frame to the room’s frame,

\[T_a(p) = R(\theta)\, p + \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}, \qquad R(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}.\]

Going the other way, from the room to the robot, undoes it: \(T_a^{-1}(q) = R(\theta)^\top (q - (x, y))\). That is the formula in the step above.

Two operations on poses come up in every later part:

operation written meaning used for
composition \(a \oplus b\) pose \(b\), given in \(a\)’s frame, in the room chaining frames; adding a step of odometry
relative pose \(a \ominus b\) pose \(b\) as seen from pose \(a\) how far the robot moved between two moments

What’s still missing

  • We assumed the robot knows its pose. It doesn’t. Every later part is, one way or another, about estimating it.
  • We moved the robot by decree. A real robot moves by turning its wheels. Part 2 works out exactly how two wheel speeds become a motion of the whole robot.

Going deeper

Homogeneous transforms

Composition is easier to write with a 3 × 3 matrix. Add a 1 under every point, \((p_x, p_y, 1)\), and write the pose as

\[T = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & x \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.\]

Then moving a point is one matrix product, \(T p\), and chaining frames is a product of matrices: \(T_{\text{map}\to\text{laser}} = T_{\text{map}\to\text{odom}}\, T_{\text{odom}\to\text{base}}\, T_{\text{base}\to\text{laser}}\). The inverse is

\[T^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} R^\top & -R^\top t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.\]

ROS’s tf2 library does exactly this, in 3-D with 4 × 4 matrices, for every frame on the robot, many times a second.

Conventions

Robots break in confusing ways when two pieces of code disagree on a convention. ROS fixes them in REP 103:

  • SI units: metres, seconds, radians.
  • Right-handed frames. On the robot, \(x\) forward, \(y\) left, \(z\) up.
  • Angles anticlockwise when seen from above (from \(+z\)).

Cameras are the exception: the optical frame has \(z\) forward, \(x\) right and \(y\) down, the way image rows run. We’ll meet it in part 11.

Angles wrap around

A heading of 179° and one of −179° are 2° apart, not 358°. Every time code subtracts two angles, it has to wrap the result back into \((-\pi, \pi]\):

\[\operatorname{wrap}(\alpha) = \alpha - 2\pi \left\lfloor \frac{\alpha + \pi}{2\pi} \right\rfloor.\]

Forgetting it is one of the classic robot bugs: the robot spins a full turn the long way round, or a filter decides it is wildly wrong whenever it faces west.

Three dimensions

A drone or a robot arm needs six numbers: position \((x, y, z)\) and orientation (roll, pitch, yaw). Writing orientation as three angles runs into trouble at some poses (gimbal lock), so ROS stores it as a quaternion, four numbers \((x, y, z, w)\) with \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2 = 1\). For a robot on a flat floor, only yaw is non-zero, and the quaternion is \((0, 0, \sin\frac\theta2, \cos\frac\theta2)\).

Further reading

  • R. Siegwart, I. Nourbakhsh and D. Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed., 2011): the standard textbook; chapter 3 covers frames and kinematics.
  • K. Lynch and F. Park, Modern Robotics (2017): rigid-body motions and homogeneous transforms, with free videos.
  • ROS REP 105, Coordinate Frames for Mobile Platforms, and REP 103, Standard Units of Measure and Coordinate Conventions.
  • T. Foote, tf: The transform library (2013): how ROS keeps the tree of frames.

entry.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 10: ROS 2, how the pieces talk

link.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 10: ROS 2, how the pieces talk

entry.content:
Series · Mobile robots from scratch 1What a mobile robot is 2Wheels and kinematics 3What a sensor is 4Encoders and odometry 5Motors and PID control 6The microcontroller: ESP32 7The onboard computer: Raspberry Pi and Jetson 8Lidar: how it measures 9Lidar: processing a scan 10ROS 2 11Depth cameras 12Sensor fusion with Kalman filters 13Localisation with particle filters 14SLAM 15Path planning and navigation

Part 7 described a robot’s software as a crowd of small programs, and part 9 wrote one of them. ROS 2 (the Robot Operating System) is how almost every research and many commercial robots connect those programs. Despite the name, it isn’t an operating system: it’s a library for passing messages, a set of tools, and thousands of packages that already do most of what this series describes.

This part is about the few ideas in it that change how a robot behaves.

How the pieces talk, step by step

Each program is a node, and nodes talk by publishing messages on named topics. The lidar driver publishes on /scan; anything that wants scans subscribes to /scan. Neither side knows the other: the driver doesn’t care whether one node listens or five, or none.

Each topic has a message type, fixed in advance: /scan carries sensor_msgs/LaserScan, /cmd_vel carries a geometry_msgs/Twist (forward speed and turn rate, part 3’s \(v\) and \(\omega\)). That contract is what lets you swap one lidar’s driver for another’s without touching anything else.

Two other ways to talk exist for jobs that aren’t a stream: a service is a request with one reply (“save the map”); an action is a long job with progress and the option to cancel (“drive to the kitchen”).

Underneath, ROS 2 sends messages with DDS (or Zenoh), and each topic chooses its quality of service (QoS). The first choice is what to do when a message is lost, which happens all the time over Wi-Fi.

Best effort sends each message once, ten scans a second. Here, with 10% lost, 8 of 100 scans never arrive, and the rest take about 5 ms. Reliable resends until each message gets through: none are lost, but the delay is now 6.5 ms on average and 45 ms at worst, and a resent message holds up the ones behind it. At 30% loss, best effort loses 33 scans, and reliable’s worst delay reaches 105 ms.

For sensor data, a lost scan doesn’t matter: the next one comes in 100 ms, and it’s newer. So drivers publish sensor data best effort. Maps, commands and anything sent once go reliable.

The two must match. A subscriber that asks for reliable gets nothing from a best-effort publisher, with only a warning. This is the most common reason a topic “has no data”.

The second choice is the history depth: how many messages to keep waiting for a subscriber that’s busy. It’s part 7’s queue again.

A node takes 40 ms on each of 30 frames a second. With a depth of 10, a common default in examples, it falls behind until the queue is full, and then every result is about 360 ms old: the robot sees the room as it was a third of a second ago. With a depth of 1, it skips frames, uses 249 of 300, and each result is about 57 ms old.

Slide the depth: every extra message kept adds about a frame’s worth of delay, 33 ms. For data where only the newest matters, keep 1.

Part 1’s frames are kept by tf2: each node publishes the transforms it knows, and any node can ask for any transform between two frames. Two of them matter most.

The odometry (the EKF of part 12) publishes odom → base_link: the robot’s pose by its wheels and IMU. It’s smooth and never jumps, but it drifts: here, part 4’s faulty wheels, 27.3 cm off after a lap (orange). The localiser (parts 13 and 14) doesn’t fix that pose. It publishes map → odom: where the whole odometry frame sits in the map. The two together put the robot where it really is (blue). Scroll to drive the lap.

Controllers use the odom frame, which is smooth; planners use the map frame, which is right. The odom frame starts where the robot started. After the lap, the localiser has moved it 27.3 cm and turned it 8.0°: exactly the wheels’ error, undone in one transform, while odom → base_link stayed smooth.

Every sensor message carries a stamp: the time it was measured. That matters because tf2 keeps every transform for the last 10 seconds, and can give the robot’s pose at any moment in between.

To place a scan in the room, a node must ask for the transform at the scan’s stamp, not the newest one. Here the robot drives at 0.4 m/s and turns at 1 rad/s. Look the pose up 50 ms late and the points land 16.8 cm off on average, 33.4 cm at worst; even 10 ms late puts them 3.4 cm off. It’s part 9’s skew, made by software.

If the transform for the stamp hasn’t arrived yet, the right answer is to wait for it a little (tf2’s MessageFilter does this), not to use the old one.

A node, in code

A complete node in Python that subscribes to scans, with sensor QoS, and publishes a speed command that slows the robot down as the nearest obstacle in front gets closer:

import math

import rclpy
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan


class Cautious(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("cautious")
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, "/cmd_vel", 10)
        # best effort, depth 5: matches what lidar drivers publish
        self.create_subscription(LaserScan, "/scan", self.on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data)

    def on_scan(self, scan):
        ahead = [
            r
            for i, r in enumerate(scan.ranges)
            if abs(scan.angle_min + i * scan.angle_increment) < math.radians(20)
            and scan.range_min < r < scan.range_max
        ]
        nearest = min(ahead, default=scan.range_max)
        cmd = Twist()
        cmd.linear.x = max(0.0, min(0.4, 0.5 * (nearest - 0.3)))  # stop 30 cm away
        self.pub.publish(cmd)


rclpy.init()
rclpy.spin(Cautious())

Run it with ros2 run, or start many nodes at once with a launch file. Then the command-line tools show what’s happening: ros2 topic list, ros2 topic hz /scan (is it really 10 Hz?), ros2 topic info -v /scan (whose QoS doesn’t match?), and ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames (is the tf tree connected?). RViz draws scans, maps, paths and frames in 3-D, and ros2 bag record saves topics to replay later, so you can test a change on yesterday’s data.

Distributions

ROS 2 has a new release every May, named in alphabetical order; those in even years are supported for five years. As of October 2026:

release out supported until Ubuntu
Humble Hawksbill May 2022 May 2027 22.04
Jazzy Jalisco May 2024 May 2029 24.04
Kilted Kaiju May 2025 November 2026 24.04
Lyrical Luth May 2026 May 2031 26.04

For a new robot, use the newest long-term release your computer’s Ubuntu supports: Lyrical on Ubuntu 26.04, or Jazzy on 24.04, which is what many boards’ images still ship.

What’s still missing

  • The depth camera, the other sensor most robots have: part 11.
  • The nodes that publish odom → base_link and map → odom. Fusing the wheels with an IMU is part 12; localising on a map, part 13.

Going deeper

DDS, Zenoh and discovery

ROS 2 doesn’t send messages itself: it hands them to a middleware through a layer called the RMW. The default is eProsima’s Fast DDS; Cyclone DDS and, since Kilted, Zenoh are also fully supported. DDS nodes find each other by discovery, sending multicast messages on the local network. That’s why two robots on one network see each other’s topics (set a different ROS_DOMAIN_ID for each), and why discovery can struggle on Wi-Fi networks that block or drop multicast. Zenoh instead uses a router that nodes connect to, which tends to be easier over Wi-Fi and the internet.

micro-ROS on the ESP32

The ESP32 of part 6 can be a ROS node too, with micro-ROS: a small version of the ROS 2 client library that runs on FreeRTOS. It talks over serial or Wi-Fi to a micro-ROS agent on the main computer, which relays its messages into the ROS graph. Then /cmd_vel arrives on the microcontroller as a normal subscription, and wheel ticks leave as a normal topic. Keep the messages small: part 6 showed a full Odometry message is too big for a serial link at 50 Hz.

Executors and callbacks

A node’s callbacks run when spin calls them, from an executor. The default runs one callback at a time, so a slow scan callback delays a timer in the same node. Give slow work its own node or callback group, with a multi-threaded executor, so the control loop’s timer isn’t kept waiting.

Further reading

  • S. Macenski et al., Robot Operating System 2: Design, architecture, and uses in the wild (Science Robotics, 2022): why ROS 2 is built the way it is.
  • ROS 2 documentation, Quality of Service settings: every QoS policy, and which combinations are compatible.
  • W. Meeussen, REP 105: Coordinate frames for mobile platforms: the map, odom and base_link convention.
  • T. Foote, tf: The transform library (TePRA 2013): how transforms are stored and looked up in time.
  • Open Robotics, ROS 2 Lyrical Luth released (May 2026).

entry.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 11: depth cameras

link.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 11: depth cameras

entry.content:
Series · Mobile robots from scratch 1What a mobile robot is 2Wheels and kinematics 3What a sensor is 4Encoders and odometry 5Motors and PID control 6The microcontroller: ESP32 7The onboard computer: Raspberry Pi and Jetson 8Lidar: how it measures 9Lidar: processing a scan 10ROS 2 11Depth cameras 12Sensor fusion with Kalman filters 13Localisation with particle filters 14SLAM 15Path planning and navigation

Part 8’s lidar sees one flat slice of the room. Anything above or below that slice, a table top, a step down, a toy on the floor, is invisible to it. A depth camera measures a distance for every pixel of an image, so it sees the room in 3-D, at the cost of range and precision.

Seeing in depth, step by step

A depth image looks like a photo, but each pixel holds a distance instead of a colour: how far the surface seen by that pixel is, along the camera’s axis. Here, near is orange and far is blue.

This camera is 30 cm above the floor on the robot of part 1, looking straight ahead, with an 87° wide view. Its image is small, 96 × 60 pixels, so each pixel is visible; real ones have about 640 × 480 or more. The pixel in the centre sees the box, 1.60 m away. At the bottom is the floor, from 51 cm in front of the robot; nearer than that is out of view.

About a fifth of the 5,760 pixels have no reading: the wall at the far end, beyond the camera’s 6 m range. Depth cameras see less far than lidars.

The most common depth camera is two cameras side by side, like two eyes. A point near the camera appears in quite different places in the left and right images; a far one, in nearly the same place. That shift, the disparity \(d\), gives the depth, by the same triangle as part 8’s triangulation lidar:

\[z = \frac{f\,b}{d}.\]

With images 848 pixels wide, \(f\) is 447 pixels. With a baseline \(b\) of 5 cm, the box at 1.60 m shifts by 14 pixels.

And it has the same weakness: error grows with the square of the distance. If the shift is found to a tenth of a pixel, the error is 0.45 cm at 1 m and 7.2 cm at 4 m. A wider baseline helps: 3.8 cm at 4 m with 9.5 cm between the cameras, 3.0 cm with 12 cm. That’s why cameras made for longer range are wider.

To find the disparity, the camera takes a small window around each pixel of the left image and slides it along the same row of the right image, looking for where it matches best. Here the window is 15 pixels wide.

On a patterned surface, one shift matches far better than any other: 14 pixels, the right answer, with the next best 3.6 times worse. Switch to a plain wall. Every shift looks the same, and the best is only 3% better than the rest: it picks 27 pixels, which would put the wall at 0.83 m instead of 1.60 m. Plain walls are exactly what rooms are made of.

The fix is active stereo: a small projector covers the scene in random infrared dots, invisible to people, which give every surface a texture. With the projector on, the plain wall matches at 14 pixels again, 4 times better than the next best. The same projector, in daylight outdoors, is drowned out by the sun, but outdoor scenes usually have texture of their own.

Each pixel with a depth is a point in 3-D. Pixel \((u, v)\) at depth \(z\) is at

\[x = \frac{(u - c_x)\,z}{f}, \qquad y = \frac{(v - c_y)\,z}{f}\]

in the camera’s frame, with \((c_x, c_y)\) the centre of the image. Then the camera’s pose on the robot, and the robot’s in the room, place it in the world, as for a lidar scan. The result is a point cloud: here about 4,650 points, seen from above.

Most points are floor (grey, about 2,300) or too high to matter (blue, about 1,500: the upper walls, the pillar). The 844 in red are between 3 cm and 50 cm above the floor: in the robot’s way.

On the floor in front of the robot is a toy, 8 cm high. The lidar’s beam is 20 cm up, so it passes over the toy: none of its points (green) are on it. To the lidar, and to any map built from it, the path is clear.

The depth camera puts 59 points on the toy. A navigation stack keeps these in its costmap (part 15) as obstacles, alongside the lidar’s. Tables are the same problem from the other side: a lidar sees only their legs, while the top, at the height of the robot’s head, is what it would hit.

This is why most robots carry both: the lidar for long range and for localising, where one precise slice is enough; the depth camera for what’s near and not in that slice.

Three ways to measure depth

  • Passive stereo: two cameras, no light of their own. Works outdoors and at range, given texture; fails on plain surfaces and in the dark.
  • Active stereo: two cameras and a dot projector. Works on plain walls indoors; outdoors it becomes passive stereo.
  • Structured light: one camera and a projector of a known pattern. The camera sees how the pattern is shifted, which is triangulation with the projector in place of the second camera. The original Kinect worked this way. Precise up close, but the pattern fades with distance and in sunlight.
  • Time of flight: part 8’s phase-shift method, measured for every pixel of a special sensor at once. Its error grows more slowly with distance, and it doesn’t need texture. But light bouncing off two surfaces before returning (multipath) makes corners read too far, and bright sunlight swamps it.

Cameras you’ll meet

As of October 2026, from the makers’ specifications:

camera method baseline or range
RealSense D435i active stereo 5 cm baseline
RealSense D455 active stereo 9.5 cm baseline
Stereolabs ZED 2i passive stereo 12 cm baseline
Orbbec Femto Bolt time of flight 0.25 to 5.5 m

RealSense was spun out of Intel as its own company in 2025. Most have an IMU and a colour camera built in, and all have ROS 2 drivers that publish the depth image, the colour image and the point cloud.

What’s still missing

  • Fusing everything. The robot now has wheels, an IMU, a lidar and a depth camera, each with its own errors. Combining them is part 12.
  • Using the points. How obstacles from both sensors go into one costmap is part 15.

Going deeper

Calibration

Every number above assumes the camera’s intrinsics (the focal length \(f\) and centre \((c_x, c_y)\), and the lens’s distortion) and, for stereo, the exact pose of one camera relative to the other. They’re measured by photographing a checkerboard from many angles, and makers calibrate at the factory. A stereo camera that’s been dropped can lose depth accuracy because its two cameras have moved by a fraction of a millimetre. The camera’s pose on the robot, its extrinsics (the base_link → camera_link transform), must be measured too: a 1° error in its tilt puts a point 4 m away 7 cm too high or low, enough to see the floor as an obstacle.

Flying pixels

At the edge of an object, a pixel sees partly the object and partly the wall behind it. Stereo matching and time of flight both tend to report a depth somewhere in between, so the cloud gets a trail of points floating in mid-air along every edge. Filters drop points whose depth differs a lot from their neighbours’.

Learned depth

Neural networks can estimate depth from a single colour image, or improve a stereo camera’s depth where matching fails. Modern stereo networks give dense, clean depth even on plain surfaces, and run on a Jetson (part 7). They can be confidently wrong, though, on things unlike what they were trained on, so robots still treat their output with care.

Further reading

  • D. Scharstein and R. Szeliski, A taxonomy and evaluation of dense two-frame stereo correspondence algorithms (IJCV 2002): how stereo matching works, and how to compare matchers.
  • L. Keselman et al., Intel RealSense stereoscopic depth cameras (CVPR workshops 2017): the design of an active stereo camera, and its error.
  • M. Hansard et al., Time-of-flight cameras: principles, methods and applications (Springer, 2013): how ToF cameras work, and multipath.

entry.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 12: sensor fusion with Kalman filters

link.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 12: sensor fusion with Kalman filters

entry.content:
Series · Mobile robots from scratch 1What a mobile robot is 2Wheels and kinematics 3What a sensor is 4Encoders and odometry 5Motors and PID control 6The microcontroller: ESP32 7The onboard computer: Raspberry Pi and Jetson 8Lidar: how it measures 9Lidar: processing a scan 10ROS 2 11Depth cameras 12Sensor fusion with Kalman filters 13Localisation with particle filters 14SLAM 15Path planning and navigation

Odometry (part 4) is smooth but drifts. A measurement of something in the room, a beacon, a wall, a landmark, doesn’t drift, but it’s noisy and only comes now and then. Neither is good enough alone. The Kalman filter combines them, and it does more than average them: it keeps track of how uncertain the robot is, and uses that to decide how much to trust each new piece of information.

Fusing what the robot knows, step by step

A robot is in a corridor. Its odometry says it’s 2.00 m along, give or take 20 cm (orange: one standard deviation, \(\sigma\), of 20 cm). A range sensor measures 2.30 m, give or take 10 cm (purple). Where is it?

Not halfway. The measurement is more precise, so it should count for more. The best combination weights each guess by how certain it is:

\[\hat x = x_{\text{odo}} + K\,(z - x_{\text{odo}}),\] \[K = \frac{\sigma_{\text{odo}}^2}{\sigma_{\text{odo}}^2 + \sigma_z^2}.\]

Here the Kalman gain \(K\) is 0.80, so the answer is 2.24 m. And it’s more certain than either guess: \(\sigma\) = 8.9 cm (green). Slide the measurement’s \(\sigma\) up to 20 cm and the gain drops to 0.50: the answer moves halfway. At 40 cm, it barely moves, to 2.06 m. Combining two guesses never makes things worse, as long as their \(\sigma\)s are honest.

Now the robot drives down the corridor, 5 cm a step for 200 steps, and the filter repeats two moves.

Predict: add the step the wheels report. The estimate moves, and its uncertainty grows, because each step adds 1 cm of wheel error. Correct: whenever there’s a measurement (here \(\sigma\) = 5 cm), fuse it as before. The uncertainty shrinks.

Measuring every 10 steps, the filter’s \(\pm 2\sigma\) band (grey) grows between measurements and snaps back at each one: a sawtooth that never gets wider than 9 cm. After 10 m, odometry alone is 20.8 cm off; the filter, 0.7 cm. Slide to never: the filter is then just odometry, and its \(\sigma\) grows as the square root of the distance, to 14 cm.

In 2-D, the robot’s state is its pose, \((x, y, \theta)\), and its uncertainty is a 3 × 3 covariance matrix. The green ellipse is its 2-σ region: where the filter thinks the robot is, about 86% sure (that’s what 2σ means in two dimensions), if it’s honest.

The robot drives round the room with wheels 5% noisy, and measures the range and bearing to five known beacons (purple) within 4.5 m, once a second. The dashed lines are the beacons it measures. A range and bearing aren’t a simple function of \((x, y, \theta)\): they involve square roots and angles. The extended Kalman filter (EKF) handles that by approximating them as straight lines around the current estimate.

Scroll to drive the lap. The ellipse stretches along the way the robot can’t measure well and shrinks with each fix. Odometry (orange, dashed) ends 60 cm off; the filter (green) stays within 8.4 cm all the way round, 3.0 cm on average.

Slide the beacons’ range down. With 3 m, the robot sees fewer beacons, less often, and the filter is 4.9 cm off on average, 18.8 cm at worst. With 1 m, it sees one only near a corner: 8.0 cm on average, and the ellipse balloons between corners. At 0, it’s odometry: 32.8 cm on average.

Notice that the ellipse grows when it should. That’s the filter’s most useful output: not just where the robot is, but how sure it is, so a planner can slow down or a localiser can look harder.

The filter only knows the noise it’s told. Here the wheels are really 5% noisy. Tell the filter they’re 10 times better than that, and it trusts them too much: the beacons barely move it, it’s 4.6 cm off on average, and the truth is inside its ellipse only 36% of the time. An overconfident filter is the dangerous kind, because it’s wrong and sure of it.

Tell it the wheels are 10 times worse, and it’s 5.3 cm off: it jumps to every noisy beacon reading. Its ellipse is too big, 99% of the time, which is safe but wasteful. Told the truth, it’s 3.0 cm off and inside 93% of the time.

Real tuning means measuring each sensor’s noise (part 3), and then checking that the errors fit inside the ellipses as often as they should.

The filter, in full

For a state \(x\) with covariance \(P\), a motion \(u\) with noise \(Q\), and a measurement \(z\) with noise \(R\):

Predict, with \(f\) the motion model and \(F\) its derivative (its Jacobian):

\[x \leftarrow f(x, u), \qquad P \leftarrow F P F^\top + Q.\]

Correct, with \(h\) what the measurement should be from \(x\), and \(H\) its Jacobian:

\[K = P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1},\] \[x \leftarrow x + K\,(z - h(x)), \qquad P \leftarrow (I - K H)\,P.\]

That’s all of it. The 1-D example above is the same equations with every matrix a single number, and \(F = H = 1\). For a linear \(f\) and \(h\) and Gaussian noise, this is the best possible estimate; for the robot’s nonlinear ones, the EKF is an approximation that works well as long as the uncertainty stays small.

On a real robot

Most ROS robots don’t use beacons. They run an EKF that fuses the wheels with the IMU: the gyro measures turning far better than the difference between two wheels that slip (parts 3 and 4), and the wheels measure forward speed without the gyro’s drift. The ROS package robot_localization does this; it publishes the odom → base_link transform of part 10. A second instance can add GPS outdoors, publishing map → odom.

Indoors, the “measurement in the room” is usually the lidar against a map, which is part 13.

What’s still missing

  • Many possibilities at once. A Kalman filter holds one guess and its ellipse. If the robot doesn’t know where it is at all, or two places look the same, one ellipse can’t describe that. Particle filters can: part 13.
  • No map to measure against. The beacons here were at known places. Building the map while localising is SLAM, part 14.

Going deeper

Why the Jacobians?

A Gaussian stays Gaussian when passed through a straight-line function, which is what keeps the Kalman filter’s equations exact. The EKF replaces \(f\) and \(h\) by their tangent lines at the current estimate. For range to a beacon at \((b_x, b_y)\), \(h = \sqrt{(b_x - x)^2 + (b_y - y)^2}\), so the row of \(H\) is \(\big[-(b_x - x)/h,\ -(b_y - y)/h,\ 0\big]\): a range tells the robot about its position along the line to the beacon, and nothing about its heading. That’s why the ellipse narrows towards the beacons it measures.

The unscented Kalman filter

Instead of a tangent line, the UKF pushes a few carefully chosen points (sigma points) through the real nonlinear function and fits a Gaussian to where they land. It needs no Jacobians, and handles stronger nonlinearity better; robot_localization offers both.

Outliers

A Kalman filter believes every measurement it’s given, weighted by \(R\). A wrong one, a beacon mistaken for another, pulls the estimate away. The usual guard is a gate: compute how far the measurement is from what was expected, in units of its uncertainty (the Mahalanobis distance, with \(H P H^\top + R\)), and ignore it if that’s too far.

Further reading

  • R. E. Kalman, A new approach to linear filtering and prediction problems (1960): the original paper.
  • S. Thrun, W. Burgard and D. Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (MIT Press, 2005), chapters 3 and 7: Kalman filters and EKF localisation, with the derivations.
  • T. Moore and D. Stouch, A generalized extended Kalman filter implementation for the Robot Operating System (IAS 2014): the robot_localization package.

entry.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 13: localisation with particle filters

link.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 13: localisation with particle filters

entry.content:
Series · Mobile robots from scratch 1What a mobile robot is 2Wheels and kinematics 3What a sensor is 4Encoders and odometry 5Motors and PID control 6The microcontroller: ESP32 7The onboard computer: Raspberry Pi and Jetson 8Lidar: how it measures 9Lidar: processing a scan 10ROS 2 11Depth cameras 12Sensor fusion with Kalman filters 13Localisation with particle filters 14SLAM 15Path planning and navigation

Part 12’s Kalman filter keeps one guess of where the robot is, with an ellipse around it. That works when the robot roughly knows where it is. But switch a robot on in a room it has a map of, and it has no idea: it could be anywhere, facing any way. And in a building of identical corridors, it might be in one of two places, which no single ellipse can describe.

A particle filter describes it with hundreds of guesses instead, and lets the lidar sort them out. On a robot with a map, this is Monte Carlo localisation (MCL), and in ROS it’s the AMCL node most robots use.

Finding itself, step by step

The robot knows the map of the room, but not where it is in it. So it makes 400 guesses, called particles: each one a full pose \((x, y, \theta)\), scattered at random over the free floor, facing random ways (red).

Together they describe what the robot believes. Where particles are dense, the robot is likely to be. Here they’re everywhere, so it could be anywhere.

The robot takes a scan (blue: 24 beams). For each particle, it asks: if I were there, facing that way, what would the lidar see? It casts the same 24 beams on the map from the particle’s pose, and compares them with the real ranges. The closer they agree, the higher the particle’s weight:

\[w \propto \prod_{\text{beams}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(r_{\text{map}} - r_{\text{real}})^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\]

Most guesses are nowhere near and get almost no weight (grey). One scan is nearly decisive: the effective number of particles, which counts how many share the weight, is down to 1, and the heaviest, with 99% of the weight, is 89 cm from the robot: not exact, but in the right part of the room. The other large red dot, with almost all the rest, is a place across the room where the scan happens to look similar.

Then the filter repeats three moves each time the robot moves and scans:

  1. Move every particle by the odometry step, plus random noise as large as odometry’s errors (part 4), so the cloud spreads as uncertainty grows.
  2. Weigh each one against the new scan.
  3. Resample: draw a new set of 400 particles, picking each from the old set in proportion to its weight. Heavy particles are copied many times; light ones vanish.

Scroll to drive the robot along the room. The cloud collapses onto one place, then follows the robot. After 8 scans the best guess is within 20 cm; after 23, it’s 1.1 cm from the truth. The particles are a few centimetres apart, which is how sure the filter is.

Enough particles must land near the truth at the start, or the filter settles on a wrong place that looks similar. Slide the number.

With 100, there’s no particle close enough, and the filter settles 5.2 m away, sure and wrong. With 200, it ends 72 cm off. With 400 it converges after 8 scans, and with 1,000 after 5. These results change from run to run: with few particles, success is a matter of luck.

The cost grows with the number: each particle casts every beam on the map, every scan. Real localisers use thousands of particles while lost and shrink to a few hundred once they’re sure (KLD sampling), and draw the first guesses near a pose the user gives in RViz when they can.

Someone carries the robot to the far corner of the room. The wheels didn’t turn, so the odometry says it hasn’t moved. Every particle is now in the wrong place, and none is near the truth. Scroll on: the filter is lost (the best particle’s scan fits the map badly, by 1.7 m), but it has no way to find the right place, and drifts off, 6.3 m away by the end.

This is the kidnapped robot problem. The fix: when the scans fit badly, replace some particles, here 10%, with fresh random ones every scan. Press the button. Most fresh particles are wrong, but sooner or later one lands near the truth, its weight is high, and resampling multiplies it. Here the filter is back within 25 cm about 10 scans after the move.

The same trick recovers from any wrong answer, which is why AMCL does it automatically, adding more random particles the worse the recent scans fit.

Particles versus a Kalman filter

  Kalman filter particle filter
belief one Gaussian any shape
lost at the start can’t can
two possible places can’t can
cost tiny grows with particles

A Kalman filter is cheap and smooth, and good at tracking a robot that knows roughly where it is. A particle filter can represent anything, at the cost of many ray casts per scan. On a robot, both run together: part 12’s EKF fuses wheels and IMU into smooth odometry (odom → base_link), and AMCL corrects it against the map (map → odom, part 10).

What’s still missing

  • The map. Everything here assumed a map of the room. Building one, while localising in it at the same time, is SLAM: part 14.
  • Going somewhere. Knowing where it is, the robot can now plan a route: part 15.

Going deeper

Faster weighing: the likelihood field

Casting every beam on the map for every particle is slow. AMCL’s default likelihood field model doesn’t cast rays at all: it precomputes, for every cell of the map, the distance to the nearest wall. To weigh a particle, it puts each beam’s end point on the map from the particle’s pose and looks up that distance: a lookup per beam instead of a walk along it. It’s less exact, since it ignores what’s between, but much faster and smoother.

Why resample, and why not too often

Without resampling, after a few scans one particle holds all the weight and the rest are wasted (degeneracy). But resampling also loses variety: copies of one particle are identical until the next motion spreads them. So filters resample only when the effective number of particles,

\[N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{1}{\sum_i w_i^2},\]

falls below a threshold, here half the particles, and use low-variance resampling, which picks with one random number and evenly spaced pointers rather than 400 independent draws.

When the map is wrong

Real rooms change: chairs move, doors open, people walk past. A beam that hits a person gives a short range the map doesn’t predict. Beam models include a chance of such short readings, and of max-range misses, so one surprising beam doesn’t sink an otherwise good particle. In this page’s model, each beam’s error is capped at 1.5 m for the same reason.

Further reading

  • F. Dellaert, D. Fox, W. Burgard and S. Thrun, Monte Carlo localization for mobile robots (ICRA 1999): the method.
  • D. Fox, Adapting the sample size in particle filters through KLD-sampling (IJRR 2003): how many particles are enough.
  • S. Thrun, W. Burgard and D. Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (MIT Press, 2005), chapters 4, 6 and 8: particle filters, beam and likelihood-field models, and augmented MCL.
  • Nav2, nav2_amcl: the ROS 2 localiser.

entry.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 14: SLAM

link.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 14: SLAM

entry.content:
Series · Mobile robots from scratch 1What a mobile robot is 2Wheels and kinematics 3What a sensor is 4Encoders and odometry 5Motors and PID control 6The microcontroller: ESP32 7The onboard computer: Raspberry Pi and Jetson 8Lidar: how it measures 9Lidar: processing a scan 10ROS 2 11Depth cameras 12Sensor fusion with Kalman filters 13Localisation with particle filters 14SLAM 15Path planning and navigation

Part 13 found the robot on a map it was given. But someone had to make that map. Making it needs to know where the robot was for each scan, and knowing where the robot was needs the map. SLAM, simultaneous localisation and mapping, solves both at once.

This part builds a map of the room from one lap, four ways: with perfect poses, with odometry, with scan matching, and with scan matching plus a loop closure.

Building a map, step by step

Cut the room into 5 cm cells, 24,000 of them, and give each a probability of being occupied. At first every cell is unknown: 50%.

Each lidar beam (blue) says two things. The cells it passes through are probably free; the cell where it ends is probably occupied. The first scan makes 1,012 cells fairly sure to be free (tinted) and 89 occupied (dark).

Rather than store probabilities, a map stores log-odds, \(l = \ln \frac{p}{1 - p}\), which turns each update into an addition. Here a hit adds 0.85 and a pass subtracts 0.4:

\[p = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{l}}.\]

One hit makes a cell 70% likely occupied, two make it 85%. A person walking through leaves a few hits, and the beams that pass through later wipe them out.

Scroll to drive the lap. Here, for now, the poses are perfect. After 161 scans, 21,647 cells are free and 997 occupied: a clean map of the room.

A real robot doesn’t know its poses. Use the wheels instead: odometry, with part 12’s 5% wheel noise (orange, dashed). By the end of the 20.8 m lap, it’s 60 cm off.

Every scan is drawn where odometry says it was taken, so the walls come out doubled and smeared. Of the cells this map calls occupied, only 39% lie on a real wall.

Part 9’s scan matching does far better. Match each scan against the one before it with point-to-line ICP, every half second, and chain the motions (green). This robot has a cheaper lidar than part 9’s, with 3 cm of noise per beam. Scan matching ends 38.3 cm off, and the map is sharper: 61% of its walls are real.

But it still drifts, because each match has a small error and 160 of them add up. Nothing in the chain can notice: each match only knows the scan before it.

At the end of the lap, the robot is back where it started. Its last scan sees the same walls as its first. Matching the two (purple, dashed) gives the true motion between the first pose and the last, to within 1 cm, however much drift has built up between them. That’s a loop closure.

Now the robot has a pose graph: a node for each keyframe (green dots), an edge for each scan match between consecutive ones, and one more edge across the loop. The chain says the last pose is here; the loop edge says it’s there. They can’t both be exactly right, so spread the disagreement over every edge, finding the poses that fit all the edges best.

Press the button. One round of Gauss–Newton brings the total squared error from 15.6 to 0.02. The last pose is now 1.0 cm off; the worst, part way round, 10.0 cm, down from 40.9. And 89% of the map’s walls are real.

A loop closure is a strong claim: these two places are the same. If it’s wrong, the optimiser obeys it anyway. Here, one extra loop edge claims that a pose at the far end of the room is at the start (red, dashed: the two places it joins).

The graph tears itself apart to agree: the poses end 3.44 m off on average, and only 21% of the map’s walls are real. One bad edge has ruined a map that 161 good ones built.

So real SLAM is careful about loops. It only tries matches near where the robot thinks it is, accepts one only if the scans fit very well, and uses robust costs that stop trusting an edge that disagrees with all the others.

The pose graph

Each node is a pose \(x_i = (x, y, \theta)\). Each edge says how pose \(j\) looks from pose \(i\), \(z_{ij}\), measured by scan matching. If the poses were right, \(x_j\) seen from \(x_i\) would match \(z_{ij}\) exactly. The optimiser finds the poses that make the total disagreement smallest:

\[\min_{x} \sum_{\text{edges}} e_{ij}^\top \Omega_{ij}\, e_{ij},\] \[e_{ij} = z_{ij} \ominus (x_j \text{ seen from } x_i),\]

where \(\Omega_{ij}\) says how much each edge is trusted (its inverse covariance, part 12). Gauss–Newton linearises every edge around the current poses, solves one big sparse linear system, and repeats. The first node is held fixed, since moving the whole map changes nothing.

This is the same least squares as part 12’s Kalman filter, solved for the whole trajectory at once rather than one step at a time. That’s why it can go back and fix poses from a minute ago, which a filter can’t.

On a real robot

  slam_toolbox Cartographer
from Steve Macenski, 2018 Google, 2016
matching scan to scan and map scans into submaps
in ROS 2 Nav2’s default maintained by community
also does lifelong mapping 3-D lidar

In ROS 2, slam_toolbox is the usual choice. It takes /scan and the odom → base_link transform from part 12’s EKF, matches scans, finds loop closures, and publishes the map as an occupancy grid on /map, along with the map → odom transform (part 10). Drive the robot round once, save the map, and from then on part 13’s AMCL can localise in it.

What’s still missing

  • Going somewhere. The robot has a map and knows where it is on it. Planning a path through it, and following it without hitting anything, is part 15.

Going deeper

The front end and the back end

SLAM systems split into two halves. The front end turns sensor data into edges: scan matching, and finding loop closure candidates, often by matching the new scan against a stored map of the area rather than one old scan. The back end optimises the graph. Here the front end was ICP and the back end Gauss–Newton; real systems use faster matchers (correlative scan matching, branch and bound) and solvers that exploit the graph’s sparsity (g2o, Ceres, GTSAM).

Before graphs: EKF SLAM and FastSLAM

The first SLAM systems put the robot and every landmark in one big EKF state. The covariance grows as the square of the number of landmarks, so it only works for small maps. FastSLAM used a particle filter over paths, part 13’s idea, with a small map for each particle; gmapping, long ROS 1’s default, does this with occupancy grids. Graph-based SLAM, which keeps every pose and solves for them all, now dominates.

Visual SLAM

A camera can do the same: match features between frames instead of scans, and recognise places by their appearance to close loops. ORB-SLAM and RTAB-Map do this, and part 11’s depth cameras give them depth for each feature. They work where lidar can’t afford to go, but suffer in the dark and on blank walls.

Further reading

  • H. Durrant-Whyte and T. Bailey, Simultaneous localization and mapping: part I (IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine, 2006): the problem and its history.
  • H. Moravec and A. Elfes, High resolution maps from wide angle sonar (ICRA 1985): the occupancy grid.
  • G. Grisetti, R. Kümmerle, C. Stachniss and W. Burgard, A tutorial on graph-based SLAM (IEEE ITS Magazine, 2010): pose graphs and how to optimise them.
  • W. Hess, D. Kohler, H. Rapp and D. Andor, Real-time loop closure in 2D LIDAR SLAM (ICRA 2016): Cartographer.
  • S. Macenski and I. Jambrecic, SLAM Toolbox: SLAM for the dynamic world (JOSS 2021), and its repository.

entry.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 15: path planning and navigation

link.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 15: path planning and navigation

entry.content:
Series · Mobile robots from scratch 1What a mobile robot is 2Wheels and kinematics 3What a sensor is 4Encoders and odometry 5Motors and PID control 6The microcontroller: ESP32 7The onboard computer: Raspberry Pi and Jetson 8Lidar: how it measures 9Lidar: processing a scan 10ROS 2 11Depth cameras 12Sensor fusion with Kalman filters 13Localisation with particle filters 14SLAM 15Path planning and navigation

The robot now has a map (part 14) and knows where it is on it (part 13). The last question is the one it was built for: how does it get somewhere? Someone clicks a goal on the far side of the dividing wall. The robot must find a route that doesn’t hit anything, then drive along it, and cope when something gets in the way.

That splits into two jobs. A planner finds a path through the map, once. A controller follows it, many times a second.

From here to there, step by step

The planner doesn’t use the map directly. The robot isn’t a point: it’s 36 cm across. So it plans on a costmap, a grid of 10 cm cells where each says how bad it is for the robot’s centre to be there.

Any cell closer to an obstacle than the robot’s radius, 18 cm, is lethal (dark): the robot would touch something. Beyond that, an inflated band (orange) costs less and less, out to 50 cm more, so paths prefer to keep away from walls without being forbidden from going near them:

\[c(d) = 0.9\, e^{-3 (d - r) / 0.5}.\]

Of the room’s 6,000 cells, 1,371 are lethal and 2,446 inflated. The robot is in the corner (blue); the goal is the red dot behind the wall.

Dijkstra’s algorithm finds the cheapest path by exploring outward from the start, always taking the cheapest unexplored cell next, until it reaches the goal. Choose it and scroll: it explores 3,905 cells, in every direction, including away from the goal.

A* adds a guess of how far each cell still is from the goal, its straight-line distance \(h\), and explores the cell with the smallest cost so far plus guess:

\[f = g + h.\]

It finds the same 10.20 m path after exploring 2,103 cells. Because the straight line is never longer than the real route, A* is still guaranteed to find the cheapest path.

Multiply the guess by 3 and the search rushes at the goal: 525 cells. But the guess now overestimates, the guarantee is gone, and the path it finds costs 10% more, squeezing past the box.

Each move costs its length times \(1 + w \cdot c\), where \(c\) is the cell’s cost and \(w\) says how much the planner cares. Slide it.

At 0, only length counts: the shortest path, 8.91 m, but it skims the box and the wall with no gap at all. One bump of the localisation, and the robot hits them. At 1, the path is 9.11 m and keeps 14 cm away. At 4, 10.20 m, and 47 cm: it goes down the middle of every gap. Beyond that, nothing changes much, since the path is already as far from things as the room allows.

A good plan is not the shortest one. It’s the shortest one the robot can follow safely, with the errors it has.

The path is a list of cells; the motors want speeds. The controller turns one into the other. Pure pursuit is the simplest that works: find the point on the path one lookahead distance ahead of the robot, and drive the circular arc that reaches it. For a point at \((x, y)\) in the robot’s frame, that arc has curvature

\[\kappa = \frac{2y}{x^2 + y^2},\]

so the robot turns at \(\omega = v\kappa\) (part 2’s kinematics give the wheel speeds).

With a lookahead of 0.4 m, the robot (blue) stays 3.8 cm from the path on average, 9.1 cm at worst, and arrives in 32.4 s. Slide it longer: at 1.2 m it looks so far ahead that it cuts the corners, 37.4 cm off at worst, which on this plan eats most of the gap the planner left. Shorter tracks tighter, but on a real robot, with delays and wheel slip, too short a lookahead makes it weave.

Maps go out of date. The robot is 4.25 m along its 10.20 m path when its lidar sees a chair that wasn’t there when the map was made. Press the button.

The lidar’s points go into the costmap as new obstacles, and the chair stands right where the old plan (red, dashed) went round the end of the wall. The planner runs again from where the robot is: a new path of 7.73 m, wider round the chair and between it and the pillar, 11.98 m in all. It found that by exploring 1,330 cells, in a few milliseconds here.

Real navigation replans like this all the time, about once a second, whether anything has changed or not.

Navigation in ROS 2: Nav2

ROS 2’s navigation stack, Nav2, is built from the same parts, each a node with plugins to choose from:

part what it does choices include
costmaps static map, sensors, inflation layers: static, obstacle, voxel
planner server the whole path, about 1 Hz NavFn, Smac (A*, Hybrid-A*), Theta*
controller server wheel commands, 20 Hz or more Regulated Pure Pursuit, DWB, MPPI
behaviour tree when to plan, follow, recover the BT navigator

There are two costmaps. The global one covers the whole map from part 14, with the lidar’s obstacles added, for the planner. The local one is a few metres round the robot, updated fast from the sensors, for the controller.

A behaviour tree ties them together: plan, follow, and replan on a timer; if the robot is stuck, clear the costmaps, spin on the spot, back up, wait, and try again. Running the whole thing takes AMCL (part 13) for map → odom, the EKF (part 12) for odom → base_link, a lidar driver, and a goal clicked in RViz.

The whole robot

That’s the end of the series, and the whole stack. Wheels and their kinematics (part 2) driven by motors under PID control (part 5), from an ESP32 (part 6) that counts encoder ticks into odometry (part 4). A Pi or Jetson (part 7) running ROS 2 (part 10), with a lidar (parts 8 and 9) and a depth camera (part 11). The EKF fuses wheels and IMU (part 12); SLAM builds the map (part 14); AMCL finds the robot on it (part 13); and Nav2 plans and drives it to the goal.

Each layer only works because the one under it is honest about its errors.

Going deeper

Planning for a robot that can’t turn on the spot

A* on a grid assumes the robot can go from any cell to its neighbour. A differential drive can, roughly; a car can’t, because it can’t turn on the spot. Hybrid-A* searches over \((x, y, \theta)\) with moves that are short arcs the vehicle can really drive, and state lattice planners use precomputed motion primitives. Nav2’s Smac planner offers both.

Smarter controllers

Pure pursuit only follows the path. DWB (the dynamic window approach) samples many speed pairs, simulates each a second or two ahead, and scores them against the path, the goal and the local costmap. MPPI samples thousands of noisy trajectories and averages them, weighted by cost. Both can dodge obstacles the global plan didn’t know about without replanning. Regulated pure pursuit, Nav2’s version of this page’s controller, slows down in tight turns and near obstacles.

Sampling-based planners

On a grid, the number of cells grows with the size of the map, and much faster with the dimensions: a robot arm with seven joints can’t be gridded at all. RRT and PRM sample random states instead and connect the ones that can reach each other; RRT* keeps improving the path as it samples more. For a mobile robot on a 2-D map, grid search is usually faster and simpler.

link.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 2: wheels and kinematics

entry.content:
Series · Mobile robots from scratch 1What a mobile robot is 2Wheels and kinematics 3What a sensor is 4Encoders and odometry 5Motors and PID control 6The microcontroller: ESP32 7The onboard computer: Raspberry Pi and Jetson 8Lidar: how it measures 9Lidar: processing a scan 10ROS 2 11Depth cameras 12Sensor fusion with Kalman filters 13Localisation with particle filters 14SLAM 15Path planning and navigation

Part 1 moved the robot by decree: put it here, turn it there. A real robot moves by spinning its wheels, and the software has to work out what a given pair of wheel speeds will do to the whole robot, and which wheel speeds will make it do what it wants. That relation is the robot’s kinematics.

This part works it out for the most common design, the one in robot vacuums, the TurtleBot and most home-built robots: the differential drive.

Two wheels, step by step

A differential drive has two driven wheels on one axle, one each side, and a caster that just follows. Each wheel has its own motor. There is no steering: the robot steers by driving its wheels at different speeds, the “difference” in its name.

Our robot’s wheels are \(L = 0.22\) m apart. Each wheel’s speed, \(v_l\) for the left and \(v_r\) for the right, is how fast its contact point moves over the floor, in m/s: the wheel’s turning speed times its radius, 35 mm.

The orange arrows show the two speeds. Here both are 0.30 m/s.

When both wheels go at the same speed, both sides of the robot cover the same distance, so it drives straight. At 0.30 m/s, the robot covers 1.20 m in the 4 seconds shown. Scroll to move it.

The speed of the robot itself, \(v\), is the speed of the point midway between the wheels. It is the average:

\[v = \frac{v_l + v_r}{2}.\]

When the right wheel is faster, the right side covers more ground, and the robot curves left. With \(v_l = 0.20\) and \(v_r = 0.40\) m/s it drives a circle.

At every moment, the robot rotates about one point on the line through its axle: the instantaneous centre of rotation (ICR, purple). Both wheels go round it, on circles of different sizes. Their speeds are in proportion to their distances from it, which pins down where it is.

The robot turns at

\[\omega = \frac{v_r - v_l}{L},\]

here \(0.20 / 0.22 = 0.91\) rad/s, on a circle of radius \(R = v / \omega = 0.33\) m. Move the sliders: the ICR slides along the axle line, far away for a gentle curve, close for a tight one.

With equal and opposite speeds, \(v = 0\): the robot doesn’t go anywhere, and the ICR sits at its centre. It turns on the spot, here at \(0.40 / 0.22 = 1.82\) rad/s, about 104° a second.

This is what makes the differential drive so popular indoors. A car needs space to turn round; this robot can face any way without moving. A round robot that turns on the spot can always get out of any place it got into.

There is one motion no pair of wheel speeds gives: sliding sideways. The wheels can only roll forward and back; they don’t slide along their axle. So at every moment the robot’s velocity points along its heading.

To end up 0.50 m to its left, facing the same way, the robot has to turn left, drive 0.50 m, and turn back, about 5 seconds of manoeuvring for something a robot with omni-wheels does directly.

This is called a nonholonomic constraint: the robot can reach every pose, but not by moving in every direction. It is why planners for wheeled robots (part 15) can’t just draw a straight line to the goal.

Software doesn’t move the robot continuously. It updates the pose once per time step \(dt\), from the speeds in that step. The simplest update, Euler’s method, moves along the current heading, then turns:

\[\begin{aligned} x &\mathrel{+}= v\,dt\cos\theta \\ y &\mathrel{+}= v\,dt\sin\theta \\ \theta &\mathrel{+}= \omega\,dt \end{aligned}\]

The thin line is half a circle of radius 0.5 m, driven in 5 s. Red is Euler; green uses the heading midway through each step instead. Scroll to make the steps longer.

With \(dt = 0.1\) s, Euler ends 3.1 cm from the true end. With 0.5 s steps it’s 15.7 cm off, and with 1 s steps 31.6 cm. The midpoint version stays within 1.7 cm even then. Real robots update every 10 to 50 ms, where both are fine, but the error adds up over a long drive: use the midpoint form, or the exact arc in the box below.

The whole thing in two lines

Forward kinematics, wheel speeds to body motion:

\[v = \frac{v_l + v_r}{2}, \qquad \omega = \frac{v_r - v_l}{L}.\]

Inverse kinematics, body motion to wheel speeds, which is what the robot’s software actually needs: a planner says “go at 0.3 m/s and turn at 0.6 rad/s”, and the motor controller needs a speed for each wheel:

\[v_l = v - \frac{\omega L}{2}, \qquad v_r = v + \frac{\omega L}{2}.\]

For 0.3 m/s and 0.6 rad/s, that’s 0.234 m/s for the left wheel and 0.366 m/s for the right. In ROS, this pair \((v, \omega)\) is the geometry_msgs/Twist message on the /cmd_vel topic, and the node that converts it to wheel speeds is the diff_drive_controller.

The exact pose update. For constant speeds over a step of length \(dt\), the robot moves on an exact arc. With \(\Delta s = v\,dt\) and \(\Delta\theta = \omega\,dt\):

\[\begin{aligned} x' &= x + r\,\big(\sin\theta' - \sin\theta\big) \\ y' &= y - r\,\big(\cos\theta' - \cos\theta\big) \\ \theta' &= \theta + \Delta\theta \end{aligned}\]

with \(r = \Delta s / \Delta\theta\), the radius of the arc.

When \(\Delta\theta\) is near zero, use the straight-line step instead, to avoid dividing by zero. This is the update the simulation in this series uses.

Other ways to drive

drive steers by sideways? seen on
differential two wheel speeds no vacuums, TurtleBot
skid steer skidding both sides no tracked robots, rovers
Ackermann turning the front wheels no cars, outdoor robots
mecanum, omni rollers on the wheels yes warehouse carts

Only the car can’t turn on the spot. Skid steer uses the same formulas as the differential drive, but its wheels have to skid sideways to turn, so the effective track is wider than the real one and changes with the floor. Ackermann steering follows a bicycle model: \(\omega = v \tan\delta / \ell\), with \(\delta\) the steering angle and \(\ell\) the wheelbase. Mecanum and omni wheels have small free rollers around their rim, so they can roll sideways too: those robots are holonomic.

What’s still missing

  • We assumed the wheels turn at the speeds we asked for. A motor doesn’t. Part 5 closes the loop with a PID controller.
  • We assumed the software knows how far each wheel has turned. It has to measure that, with encoders, and turning wheel turns into a pose is odometry, part 4. First, part 3 asks what a sensor is in the first place.

Going deeper

Where the ICR is

In time \(dt\) the robot turns by \(\omega\,dt\) about the ICR, at distance \(R\) to the left of its centre. The left wheel is at distance \(R - L/2\) from the ICR, the right at \(R + L/2\), and each covers its circle at its own speed:

\[v_l = \omega\,(R - L/2), \qquad v_r = \omega\,(R + L/2).\]

Subtracting gives \(\omega = (v_r - v_l)/L\); adding gives \(v = \omega R\), so

\[R = \frac{L}{2} \cdot \frac{v_r + v_l}{v_r - v_l}.\]

Equal speeds put the ICR at infinity (straight ahead); opposite speeds put it at the centre; one wheel stopped puts it on that wheel.

The speeds the wheels allow

Each wheel has a top speed. Our motors turn the wheel at about 18 rad/s with no load, so \(\lvert v_l\rvert, \lvert v_r\rvert \le 0.63\) m/s. In terms of the body:

\[\lvert v\rvert + \frac{L}{2}\,\lvert\omega\rvert \le v_{\max}.\]

That’s a diamond in the \((v, \omega)\) plane: the robot can go straight at 0.63 m/s, spin at \(2 \times 0.63 / 0.22 = 5.7\) rad/s, or anything in between, but not both at full speed. If a planner asks for more, the controller has to scale both down together, keeping the ratio, or the robot will follow a different curve from the one planned.

Why the midpoint is so much better

Over a step, the true heading sweeps from \(\theta\) to \(\theta + \Delta\theta\). Euler uses the heading at the start for the whole step, so its error is first order: half the step’s turn, every step. The midpoint uses the average heading, so the first-order error cancels and only a second-order one is left. For \(\Delta\theta\) small, the exact arc’s chord points exactly along \(\theta + \Delta\theta/2\), and is only shorter than the arc by a factor \(\operatorname{sinc}(\Delta\theta/2) \approx 1 - \Delta\theta^2/24\). That’s why the green path above barely moves.

  • G. Dudek and M. Jenkin, Computational Principles of Mobile Robotics (3rd ed., 2024), chapter 2.
  • ROS 2 Control, diff_drive_controller: the standard implementation, with wheel separation and radius as parameters.
  • K. Lynch and F. Park, Modern Robotics, chapter 13: wheeled mobile robots, holonomic and nonholonomic.

entry.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 3: what a sensor is

link.title: mobile robots from scratch, part 3: what a sensor is

entry.content:
Series · Mobile robots from scratch 1What a mobile robot is 2Wheels and kinematics 3What a sensor is 4Encoders and odometry 5Motors and PID control 6The microcontroller: ESP32 7The onboard computer: Raspberry Pi and Jetson 8Lidar: how it measures 9Lidar: processing a scan 10ROS 2 11Depth cameras 12Sensor fusion with Kalman filters 13Localisation with particle filters 14SLAM 15Path planning and navigation

Part 2 worked out how wheel speeds move the robot. To use that, the robot has to measure its wheels, and to avoid hitting things it has to measure the room. Everything it knows comes through its sensors.

A sensor turns something physical into a number: a voltage, a count of pulses, a time. Every sensor does this imperfectly, and in the same few ways. This part is about those ways, because every algorithm in the rest of the series exists to cope with them.

Sensors and their flaws, step by step

Some sensors measure the robot, some measure the world.

Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot’s own state: how far its wheels turned, how fast it is rotating, how it is accelerating. They work anywhere, even in the dark in an empty hall, but they only say how the robot moved, never where it is.

Exteroceptive sensors measure the world around it: a bumper, a range finder, a lidar, a camera. They can tell the robot where it is, but only if there is something to see, and only if it can match what it sees to what it knows.

A good robot uses both. This series covers each kind in turn: encoders in part 4, lidar in parts 8 and 9, depth cameras in part 11, and how to combine them in part 12.

Point a range sensor at a wall 1.50 m away and read it 20 times a second for 5 seconds. You don’t get 1.50 a hundred times. You get a cloud.

Two different things are wrong with it.

  • Noise: the readings scatter, randomly, around their own average. Here their standard deviation \(\sigma\) is 1.8 cm.
  • Bias: the average itself is off, here by 3.1 cm: it sits at 1.53 m. Maybe the sensor’s zero is behind its front face, or the speed of sound was set for a colder room.

The usual words are precision for the first (how close readings are to each other) and accuracy for the second (how close they are to the truth). Move the sliders: they change the two independently.

The obvious fix is to average. The average of the first \(n\) readings is 1.53 m for one reading, 1.51 for 4, 1.52 for 16 and 1.53 for all 100.

The noise in an average of \(n\) independent readings shrinks like

\[\sigma_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},\]

the grey band. Four times as many readings halve the noise. But the average closes in on 1.50 + bias, not on 1.50. No amount of averaging removes a bias. The only cure is to calibrate: measure against something you know, and subtract the difference.

Set the bias slider to zero and the average homes in on the truth.

A robot can’t wait for 100 readings. It needs an answer every time a reading arrives. The simplest running filter is the exponential moving average:

\[\hat z \leftarrow \hat z + \alpha\,(z - \hat z).\]

Each new reading pulls the estimate a fraction \(\alpha\) of the way towards itself.

At 2.5 s, someone steps in front of the sensor, 1 m away. With \(\alpha = 0.3\) the filtered line (red) has 0.6 cm of noise left, a third of the raw 1.7 cm, and catches up with the person 0.45 s later. With \(\alpha = 0.1\) the noise drops to 0.4 cm, but it takes 1.45 s to notice. At 0.5 m/s, that’s over 70 cm of driving towards someone it hasn’t seen yet.

Every filter makes this trade. Part 12’s Kalman filter makes it as well as it can be made, by also knowing how the robot moves.

An ultrasonic sensor, like the cheap HC-SR04, sends a chirp of sound and times the echo. At 343 m/s, a wall 1.50 m away echoes back in 8.7 ms. The sound leaves in a cone about 15° either side, and the sensor reports the first echo from anywhere in it.

Facing the wall straight on, it reads 1.50 m. Turn it 35° and it reads 1.60 m, though the wall straight ahead is 1.83 m away: the echo came from the edge of the cone, where the sound hit the wall more squarely.

Turn it 60° and it reads nothing. Sound hitting a smooth wall at a steep angle bounces off like light off a mirror, away from the sensor (grey rays). A robot relying on this sensor drives straight into a wall it approaches at an angle. Try the slider.

A gyroscope measures how fast the robot turns, in degrees per second. To get the heading, the robot adds up (integrates) those readings over time.

Small MEMS gyros, like those in phones and robot IMUs, have a bias of a fraction of a degree per second, which drifts slowly with temperature. Here the robot is standing still, and the gyro’s bias is 0.5°/s. After a minute, the integrated heading says the robot has turned 29.5°.

The fix is the same as before: calibrate. If the robot stands still for its first 5 seconds and subtracts the average reading, the heading after a minute is off by only −0.6°, from the noise and the slow wander of the bias. That’s why many robots ask you not to touch them while they boot.

An accelerometer measures acceleration. Integrate once for speed, again for position. It sounds like the perfect sensor: it needs no wheels and works anywhere.

It isn’t. A bias of \(b\) in acceleration grows into a position error of \(\tfrac12 b t^2\). A bias of 0.01 m/s², about a thousandth of gravity, is a small one, yet after 1 s the position is off by 0.6 cm, after 5 s by 15.3 cm, and after 10 s by 58.9 cm.

So an accelerometer alone can’t tell a robot where it is for more than a second or two. On a ground robot it’s mainly used to find which way is down (gravity), and to catch bumps and tilts.

What to ask of any sensor

Every datasheet answers the same questions, and these are the ones that matter for a robot:

property question example
range the smallest and largest value it can measure an HC-SR04 sees about 2 cm to 4 m
resolution the smallest change it can report an encoder tick; one step of an ADC
noise how much readings scatter (σ) 1.8 cm in the figure
bias how far their average is off 3.1 cm in the figure
rate how many readings per second a lidar spins 5 to 20 times a second
latency how old a reading is when you get it a camera frame can be 30 to 100 ms old
field of view which directions it sees 30° cone; 360° plane; 87° × 58° image

The last two are easy to forget. A reading is a statement about the past: the robot has moved on since. Part 9 shows what a lidar scan looks like when this is ignored.

How sensors talk

Sensors hand their numbers to the robot’s microcontroller in a few standard ways:

  • digital pins: on or off (a bumper), or pulses to count or time (an encoder, an ultrasonic echo);
  • analog voltage, read by an ADC (analog-to-digital converter): an IR distance sensor, a battery voltage;
  • I²C and SPI: short buses for chips on the same board, like IMUs (the MPU-6050, the BNO085) and time-of-flight sensors (the VL53L1X);
  • UART (serial) and USB: for sensors that send a stream, like a lidar;
  • Ethernet: for high-bandwidth sensors, like 3-D lidars and some depth cameras.

Part 6 shows how an ESP32 reads several of these at once without dropping any.

What’s still missing

  • We measured with a sensor pointed at a wall. Part 4 builds a sensor the robot can count on everywhere: the wheel encoder, and turns its counts into a pose.
  • We met drift twice. Integrating a rate sensor (gyro, accelerometer, and next time, wheel encoders) always drifts. The cure, combining it with a sensor that sees the world, is part 12.

Going deeper

Noise models

The figure draws noise from a Gaussian (normal) distribution: \(z = d + b + \varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). That’s a good model for many sensors, for a reason: noise that comes from adding up many small independent effects tends to be Gaussian (the central limit theorem). It is also the model that makes the maths of part 12 come out in closed form.

Real sensors add other kinds of error. A range sensor sometimes returns a max-range reading when it hears no echo, or a short one when someone walks past. Part 13’s particle filter uses a sensor model that mixes a Gaussian with these, so one wild reading can’t wreck the estimate.

Why √n

If readings \(z_1, \dots, z_n\) are independent with variance \(\sigma^2\), their sum has variance \(n\sigma^2\), because variances of independent things add. Dividing by \(n\) divides the variance by \(n^2\):

\[\operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac1n \sum z_i\Big) = \frac{n \sigma^2}{n^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.\]

The standard deviation is the square root: \(\sigma / \sqrt n\). This only works for independent noise. A bias is the same in every reading, so it survives the average untouched.

The moving average’s lag

For the exponential moving average with factor \(\alpha\), after a sudden step the remaining error shrinks by a factor \((1 - \alpha)\) per reading. Closing 90% of the gap takes \(\ln 0.1 / \ln(1 - \alpha)\) readings: 6.5 for \(\alpha = 0.3\) and 22 for \(\alpha = 0.1\), which at 20 readings a second is 0.32 s and 1.09 s. (The figure’s times are longer because it waits until the estimate is within 2.5 cm, 95% of the way, through the noise.)

In steady state, the noise left over is

\[\sigma_{\hat z} = \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2 - \alpha}},\]

0.42σ for \(\alpha = 0.3\) and 0.23σ for \(\alpha = 0.1\). Smaller \(\alpha\): less noise, more lag. There is no setting that gives both.

Allan variance

Gyro datasheets describe noise with two numbers: angle random walk (white noise, in °/√h) and bias instability (how far the bias wanders, in °/h). Both come from the Allan variance: record the gyro standing still for hours, average it over windows of length \(\tau\), and see how much neighbouring windows differ. For short windows, white noise dominates and averaging helps; for long ones, the wandering bias dominates and averaging stops helping. The bottom of the curve says how long you can usefully average.

Further reading

  • S. Thrun, W. Burgard and D. Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005), chapter 6: sensor models, including the beam model with its mixture of noise, short readings and max-range readings.
  • O. Woodman, An introduction to inertial navigation (2007): why integrated gyros and accelerometers drift, and the Allan variance.
